newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Opposition leads ex-communists in Romania vote.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leads ex-communists in Romania vote.

text.p: Romania's centrist opposition maintained a healthy lead over its ex-communist foes in parliamentary elections with half the votes counted on Monday.
The Democratic Convention (CDR), which pledges swift reform to tackle widespread poverty in Romania, now looks strong enough to lead a coalition to end seven years of government by former communists.
But in the presidential race, incumbent Ion Iliescu has edged ahead, doing better than exit polls predicted.
In the presidential contest, due to go to a second round in two weeks time, Iliescu had 33 percent support to CDR leader Emil Constantinescu's 28 percent.

With 8,702 polling stations reporting to the Central Election Bureau, some 57 percent of the total, former Prime minister Petre Roman was in third place with 21 percent. His votes will play a pivotal role in the run-off.
But the CDR was well out in front in races for both houses of parliament.
In the lower Chamber of Deputies, it had just over 30 percent, compared to 22 percent for Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR). Figures for the upper house, the Senate, were broadly similar.
Roman's Social Democratic Union (USD) was third with 13 percent in both chambers and looks set to hold the balance of power in any coalition government.
Tallies for both Iliescu and the PDSR were expected to rise slightly as election officials receive figures from more remote rural areas which traditionally back the president.
Both the CDR and USD say they will not enter a coalition with the PDSR, which they say is corrupt and inept in dealing with Romania's protracted economic crisis.
But personal rivalry between the two opposition leaders blocked conclusion of any formal post-election pact.
Iliescu appealed to the CDR after exit polls were announced to consider aligning itself with his ruling party.
The ethnic Hungarian UDMR party, generally unfriendly to Iliescu, also held a pivotal position in fourth place with some six percent.
Romanian nationalist parties look to be the only other political groups scoring strongly enough to beat the three percent threshold for a place in parliament.
